set.statement: In adults who have used classic psychedelics, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything people do during a difficult experience makes it shorter or easier: no study read here tested a way of coping, and what is known is what people say helped, looking back. Two independent surveys agree only that a calming or accepting response (trying to calm the mind; letting go or accepting the experience) was the one most often named as helpful; their lists and questions differed, so their percentages cannot be compared. In a self-selected online survey of 529 people recalling a challenging experience with a classic psychedelic or an analogue (psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, DMT or mescaline; use combined with non-classic drugs such as MDMA or ketamine was allowed) (Wood et al., 2024), the responses, of 26 listed, most often tried and judged helpful were letting go, accepting or surrendering (84.5%), observing the mind without fighting it (77.3%) and closing the eyes or lying or sitting down (73.9%); the least often were directing anger at the experience (9.4%), trying to sleep (9.7%), telling it to stop (10.6%) and taking another drug or alcohol (12.1%). People who judged more of the 11 responses that the authors grouped as acceptance and reappraisal helpful rated their emotional breakthrough higher (r = 0.50), but that group also includes breathing, closing the eyes, questioning the experience, telling it to stop and directing anger at it; both were rated at one sitting, sometimes years later, and judging a response helpful may itself reflect how the experience ended. Sixteen people who had attended psilocybin retreats, chosen because their difficult ceremonies had been followed by personal change, wrote of breathing on purpose, opening their eyes and moving, engaging with the surroundings, asking for help, and facilitators' touch, listening, reassurance and reminders to breathe, among other responses. In a US online panel, 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience, ticked what had helped during their most challenging one: trying to calm the mind 257 (41.9%), changing location 168 (27.4%), asking a friend for help 124 (20.2%), changing the people around 124 (20.2%), smoking cannabis 113 (18.4%) and changing the music 99 (16.2%); fewer ticked drinking alcohol (54, 8.8%) or taking another drug (22, 3.6%) (Simonsson et al., 2023). No study tested any of these responses, including taking cannabis, alcohol or another drug, which in the other survey was among the responses least often judged helpful (12.1%). As summarized second-hand in a mini review (Piercey et al., 2024), 91% of respondents to an earlier survey of difficult experiences with psilocybin mushrooms used at least one such strategy and rated them only modestly effective, and 65.9% of surveyed callers to a psychedelic peer-support phone line (the drugs they had taken are not stated) said it helped ease their distress. None of these studies compared people who did something with people who did not. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Looking back, people most often said that letting go, watching their thoughts without fighting them, calming the mind, or closing their eyes and lying down helped during a difficult trip; moving somewhere else or asking a friend also came up. None of the studies tested whether any of these actually helps: no study compared people who did them with people who did not.
set.magnitude: No effect estimates. Tried and judged helpful (Wood et al., 2024; n = 529): letting go 84.5%, observing the mind 77.3%, closing the eyes or lying down 73.9%; least often anger 9.4%, trying to sleep 9.7%, telling it to stop 10.6%, another drug or alcohol 12.1%. Count of the 11 responses grouped as acceptance and reappraisal judged helpful, against emotional breakthrough rated at the same sitting: r = 0.50. Ticked as helpful (Simonsson et al., 2023; n = 613, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience): calming the mind 41.9%, changing location 27.4%, asking a friend 20.2%, changing the people around 20.2%, cannabis 18.4%, changing the music 16.2%, alcohol 8.8%, another drug 3.6%. The two surveys' percentages are not comparable (different lists, questions and denominators). Second-hand (Piercey et al., 2024): 91% used strategies, rated modestly effective; 65.9% of helpline callers found it helpful.
set.population: Adults who have used classic psychedelics and recalled a challenging experience: a self-selected online sample (529), retreat attendees chosen for personal change after difficult ceremonies (16) and a US online panel (613, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience)
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: The two surveys, with different lists and questions, agree that a calming or accepting response was the one most often named as helpful.
set.grade.reasoning: Cross-sectional self-report starts low; down two for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated refers to the reports only: two independent surveys (University College London; a Karolinska, Oxford and Wisconsin team), with different lists and questions, agree that a calming or accepting response was the one most often named as helpful; no study tested whether any response works. Section 7 (decision p-before-during-after): findings only, for the senior author's approval.

set.statement: In people who use classic psychedelics outside research or therapy, evidence is insufficient to say whether harm reduction habits lower the chance of a difficult experience. The one survey read here that measured both (Palmer and Maynard, 2022; pre-registered) asked 163 self-selected, mostly male, experienced people (median 11.5 lifetime uses), reached through university societies and online psychedelic communities, to recall their first experience (a median of 42 months earlier) and their most recent one (a median of 2 months earlier): which listed practices they had used before, during and after, how challenging it had been (Challenging Experience Questionnaire) and how much emotional breakthrough it brought (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory). A score adding up the practices each person used, each weighted by how important the sample rated it for safety, correlated weakly with lower challenge for the first experience (r = −0.21, 95% CI −0.35 to −0.06) and not significantly for the most recent (r = −0.15, −0.30 to 0.00), and with more breakthrough on both occasions (r = 0.24, 0.09 to 0.38), 2 to 6% of the variation (editors' intervals and calculation). The score counted practices after the experience, which cannot have shaped it, was weighted by the respondents' own judgments, was recalled at the same sitting as the outcomes and was not adjusted for anything, and people who stopped after a difficult first experience could not take part. Scores were higher for the most recent experience (48.7 against 40.1), for practices before and after use but not during it, while challenge scores were about the same (17.1 and 17.3% of the maximum). Most were with trusted friends, a practice the sample rated important; few had a sober sitter, which it rated low; and few tested their drugs, although testing was rated important. In a US online panel, 182 of 613 people (29.7%) linked their most challenging experience to having had no preparation; that link went with slightly higher challenge ratings for the same experience, rated at the same sitting (standardized beta 0.09), but not with later thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others (adjusted odds ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.45) (Simonsson et al., 2023). A mini review that relies heavily on the first survey for its outcome evidence summarizes it as more strategies going with fewer challenging experiences, which overstates it (the score was weighted, and the link with challenge held for the first experience only); the review adds a catalogue of strategies named in the literature and finds outcome research scarce: besides that survey, one preparedness-scale study of psychedelic use (drug class not stated), one ketamine study (design not stated) and, for MDMA, a rapid scoping review whose reference is a preprint, all second-hand (Piercey et al., 2024). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

set.statement: In college students, as described second-hand in a single-author narrative review of 62 published studies found up to February 2013, which pooled no data (Pearson, 2013), evidence is insufficient to say whether using more protective behavioural strategies (things people do just before, during or after drinking to limit their drinking or its harms, such as keeping track of drinks, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, eating, or using a designated driver), compared with using fewer, lowers drinking or alcohol-related problems. Students nearly always reported their strategies, drinking and problems themselves on questionnaires (at least 11 different ones), usually at one sitting and often for no stated period, so most links are associations reported by the same people, not predictions; the author estimates, without showing how, that 80% of the studies gave only cross-sectional data. By the author's account, nearly every study found that students who reported using more strategies also reported drinking less or having fewer problems, mostly as correlations whose sizes the review does not give; with one questionnaire, the link was negative when students rated how often they used strategies when they drank, but positive when they counted how many times they used them, a count that also rises with how often they drink (three studies by the author's team). In three studies, students reporting more strategies showed a weaker link between how much they drank and their problems. Over time the evidence was mixed: in a sample followed for a year after a peer intervention that showed no significant effect, correlations with later drinking were about as strong as those at the same time and changes in some kinds of strategy use went with less drinking or fewer problems, but correlations with later problems were weaker (3 of 9 not significant); in another study, strategy use rose after a brief intervention but the rise did not go with changes in drinking; and in women, strategy use was unrelated to drinking or problems at the same time point but went with fewer problems 4 months later. In two studies of day-by-day reports (a 15-day diary of 40 students, and a 7-day recall at one sitting around the 21st birthday), strategies about the way people drank went with less drinking on the days they were used, but people drank more on days they used limiting or stopping strategies, and drank more and had more problems on days with a designated driver or going home with a friend, which the author suggests reflects these strategies being planned for nights of heavy drinking. Students told to use more strategies reported using more but did not drink less (one experiment). In three trials of brief alcohol interventions, a rise in reported strategy use statistically mediated the interventions' effect on drinking or problems; in three others, the interventions did not change strategy use; none mainly targeted strategies. The author calls the trial and follow-up evidence mixed but ends by calling strategy use a promising way to reduce drinking and its harms. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
set.plain: In nearly every study of college students, those who said they used more safety habits when drinking also said they drank less or had fewer problems, but most studies asked about habits and drinking at the same time. Day by day, students drank more on days they had a designated driver or went home with a friend, which the review's author thinks happens because these are planned for nights of heavy drinking. Telling students to use more habits did not make them drink less in the one study that tried it, so whether the habits themselves lower drinking or harm is not known.
set.magnitude: No pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: nearly every study found that students reporting more strategies reported drinking less and/or fewer problems; with one questionnaire, correlations with drinking were negative on a how-often-when-drinking scale and positive on a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions (3 studies); a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; in one sample followed for 12 months, prospective correlations with drinking similar to same-time ones, change in some kinds of strategy use predicting less drinking or fewer problems, and 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant; day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Direction differs by strategy and design: less drinking between people, but more drinking and more problems day by day with serious harm reduction and limiting or stopping strategies; follow-up findings mixed; mediation in three trials and no change in strategy use in three; one null instruction experiment.

set.statement: In people who use benzodiazepines, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything they do themselves before or during use lowers harm: as described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources that did not appraise them (Morrison et al., 2025), no source compared people who used such a practice with people who did not, and none measured harm as an outcome of a practice. Practices appear as people's accounts, researchers' recommendations and reports of behaviour after drug checking: in a study of a Swedish online drug forum about flubromazolam (122 in the review's table), posters described limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they used, avoiding alcohol at the same time and comparing vendors and batches; in British Columbia during COVID-19, women and gender-diverse people who use drugs (45, in a qualitative study) formed informal peer networks to check on one another because of benzodiazepine contamination and the risk of sexual assault; in an ethnography in Melbourne, one participant described using temazepam at home to avoid losing money or drugs, or being arrested, while sedated; and the authors of a survey of 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok called for education against injecting alone. Numbers come only from two drug-checking studies, and they describe behaviour, not harm: in a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group, in which 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore received fentanyl test strips, 69% of the 68 followed up a month later reported doing something to lower harm after a result, such as asking someone to check on them, and reported using alone fell from 96% to 68%; and in an observational study of 541 adults who use drugs in several US states, a positive fentanyl test-strip result went, over 28 days, with reports of using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested (an association in the review's table, which its text words as a result of the strip). The review searched on terms such as harm reduction and did not cover peer-led resources, so practices described elsewhere may be missing; its authors find harm reduction largely absent for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: People who use benzos describe staying at home, keeping the drug out of reach while high, avoiding alcohol at the same time and having friends check on them. In two studies of fentanyl test strips, people said they took more care after a positive result, such as having someone check on them, but harm was not measured. No study found by a 2025 review compared people who do these things with people who do not, so it is not known whether any of them lowers harm.
set.magnitude: No source compared people who used a practice with people who did not, and none measured harm. Behaviour after test strips: in a before-and-after pilot (68 of 103 followed up at one month, no control group), reported using alone was 96% before and 68% after, and 69% reported a harm reduction behaviour after a result; in an observational study of 541 adults over 28 days, a positive result went with using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested (sizes given only in the review's table, second-hand).
set.population: People who use benzodiazepines, including novel ones, in forum, qualitative, ethnographic, survey, pilot and observational sources gathered by one scoping review: posters on a Swedish drug forum; 45 women and gender-diverse people who use drugs in British Columbia; one participant in Melbourne; 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok; 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore; 541 adults who use drugs in several US states
set.exposure: Practices people use themselves before or during use, as described: limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they use, avoiding alcohol at the same time, comparing vendors and batches, peer check-ins, not using or injecting alone; and reported behaviour after a test-strip result (asking someone to check on them, using smaller amounts, taking turns, keeping naloxone nearby)
set.comparator: None: no source compared people using a practice with people not using it; the two test-strip studies compared reports before and after receiving strips, or related behaviour to the strip result
set.outcome: Any harm, such as overdose, assault, injury or arrest (not measured against a comparison in any source); reported behaviour after a test-strip result
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Forum content, qualitative accounts, one ethnographic account, a survey's recommendation and two test-strip studies of reported behaviour (a before-and-after pilot without controls and an observational study); no comparison of people using a practice with people not using it; none appraised by the review (card sc_morrison_2025).

evidence_add.locator: Results › Direct interventions › Drug checking, 3rd paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Gelberg et al.)
evidence_add.extracted: Gelberg et al.: multi-state US community-based observational study of 541 adults who use drugs, recruited at fixed and mobile harm reduction services, over 28 days. Positive fentanyl test-strip results were linked to safer use (using smaller amounts, taking turns, having naloxone nearby); Table 1 gives a four-fold reduction in quantity used after a positive result, strongest when benzodiazepines were tested (20-fold), then stimulants (tenfold), weakest for opioids (twofold), as an association, while the Results text says the positive result 'resulted in' the reduction. Behaviour, not harm, was the outcome.
